newsitem.title: USA: U.S. death toll rises as Hurricane Fran downgraded.
newsitem.headline: U.S. death toll rises as Hurricane Fran downgraded.

text.p: Residents of North and South Carolina wearily faced the wreckage left by Hurricane Fran on Friday as the giant storm, which left at least 14 dead, weakened and moved inland.

The damage prompted President Bill Clinton to declare North Carolina a major disaster area. "We are going to do everything we can to help the people of North Carolina," he said in a speech in Orlando, Florida.

More than 4 million people in the Carolinas and Virginia were left without power after Fran hit land near Wilmington on Thursday night, snapping power lines, tossing signs and billboards like confetti and hurling trees into houses.

Fran's heavy rains soaked the region, causing flooding in North Carolina, Virginia and West Virginia as it headed inland. Forecasters forecast heavy rain and issued flash-flood watches through Saturday for parts of Pennsylvania and small-stream flooding in Maryland, as rains drenched much of the Middle Atlantic area and the East Coast.
In North Carolina, hundreds of roads were closed by flooding and farmers worried about flooded fields of corn, tobacco and cotton crops.

"This is the worst storm we've had in a long, long time," North Carolina Gov. Jim Hunt told reporters in Wilmington. "We've had terrible damage on the coast and that damage went all through the state."
Hunt said damage in North Carolina could run as much as $1 billion, and about one-fourth of its people had lost power.
The Insurance Information Institute said on Friday that insurors would pay about $625 million in claims to people whose property was damaged by Fran.
The damage was worst in southeastern North Carolina, where residents awoke on Friday to see fallen trees, scattered boats, signs and other debris, and some collapsed buildings.

"It's the worst storm in North Carolina since Hazel in 1954. It's so wide and so humongous," said Ben Taylor, spokesman for the North Carolina Emergency Operations Centre in Raleigh. Hazel left 95 people dead in the Carolinas.

On Topsail Beach and Surf City, two seaside communities near of Wilmington, some houses were blown into the water and there were reports that a tornado touched down. Dunes were washed away and beach erosion was widespread.

Fran was downgraded to a tropical storm before dawn on Friday, about 10 hours after its centre landed near Wilmington. It weakened further to a tropical depression as it moved inland on Friday afternoon.
Fran played a hand in the presidential election campaign as well, forcing Republican nominee Bob Dole to cancel a flight to New Jersey for a speech, a campaign spokesman said.
In some areas, as much as 15 inches (37.5 cm) of rain fell and forecasters warned that flooding in areas already soaked this summer could be the storm's most serious impact.

North Carolina officials said they had had reports of 11 deaths linked to the storm, mostly from traffic accidents and fallen trees. One of the dead was a 10-year-old boy who was killed when a tree crushed his trailer home.

South Carolina reported two deaths, but officials said five people had died in a trailer home fire and another had died in a house fire during power outages caused by Fran. Officials expressed relief the state missed Fran's worst.
One woman in Virginia also was reported dead. She was swept away by floodwaters while trying to cross a creek in an all-terrain vehicle, a government spokeswoman said.
